Learning Objectives

Identify mental health concerns specific to the athlete’s experience.

Licensed mental health practitioners manage and support the mental health and well-
being of athletes. They work in athletic departments, sporting organizations, and in
community practice. In the past decade, an increased focus on the mental health of
athletes has corresponded with increased demand for mental healthcare services.
Differentiation between mental health care and performance enhancement is important.
In addition, the effect of mental skills on physical recovery is essential. Orthopaedic
surgeons should understand some of the most common clinical conditions managed by
mental health practitioners in the athletic setting and review common mental skills.
What is Sport Psychology?
Definitions and Qualifications
The term sport psychologist often is misused.
Licensed mental health providers can provide treatment for clinical issues in addition to sport
performance training.
Sport psychology consultants can provide strategies to enhance performance.
Professionals can earn Certified Mental Performance Consultant certification through the
Association for Applied Sport Psychology.
Some professionals are qualified to do both
Mental health licensure is required.
Mental performance consultant certification is preferred but not required.
A continuum of care approach can provide the most comprehensive care.

Definitions and Qualifications
Sport psychology services include the management of mental health conditions in
athletes and strategies to improve performance. Sport psychology professionals must
have a license to practice mental health care and manage psychologic conditions. All 50
states have regulatory boards that license and oversee mental health professionals. In
addition, the Association for Applied Sport Psychology certifies professionals who have
completed the necessary coursework and passed a certification examination.

The continuum of care model is a framework that links mental health and performance
optimization. Most athletes with a mental health condition benefit from comprehensive
care addressing mental health and performance optimization. The techniques used to
manage mental health conditions and the interventions used to improve athletic
performance are quite different; however, the aspects of care often are inseparable and
are best addressed via a fluid, holistic approach.1,2
Importance of Sport Psychology in Comprehensive Care
Injury can impair mood, and impaired mood can increase injury risk.
Research supports the use of sport psychology services to supplement injury rehabilitation
programs.
Injury risk and recovery from injury are strongly affected by mental health (especially stress)3,4
(Resources 1 and 2).
Treatment and Referrals
Sport medicine physicians often are the first providers to identify athletes with
psychopathology. Unless a physician is comfortable managing the condition, referral to a sport
psychologist typically is warranted.
Knowledge of existing resources and referral processes is critical to making an effective
referral.
Proactive integration of sport psychology services in medical care aids in normalizing the use
of services, leading to more effective referral and treatment buy-in.
Interdisciplinary team
Sports medicine staff
Community resources (eg, private practice providers, college campus counseling centers)
Specialists with clinical expertise (eg, substance use, eating disorders, trauma)
In many locations, resources for consultation and referral may be limited.

Treatment and Referrals

Sports medicine physicians have a unique opportunity to proactively champion the value
of sport psychology services as part of a comprehensive rehabilitation program.
Integrated sport psychology services can be perceived as a normal aspect of care rather
than a negative consequence to injury. Great value exists in sport psychology
professionals collaborating with the interdisciplinary medical team to provide holistic
care. Given the recent focus on athletes’ mental health, many Olympic, professional, and
college organizations have created sport psychology positions. Although this is valuable
for the growth of the field, many of these positions are unfilled because there are not
enough qualified professionals, particularly those who are licensed to provide mental
health care in addition to sport performance services5 (Resource 3).
Clinical Concerns
Clinical Overview
Although improving, stigma is related to the mental health of athletes and student-athletes.
Sport psychology professionals must actively work to reduce stigma, increase openness to
treatment, and provide clinically sound treatment for clinical and performance concerns6
(Resource 4).
Mood and Anxiety Disorders
Mood and anxiety disorders require management; a combination of medication and
counseling is the most effective approach.
Mood disorders often are conceptualized as a biopsychosocial concern and may arise at any
time, especially postinjury and/or postoperatively.
Young adults are reporting increasing rates of depressive disorders.
Anxiety is increasingly common. One in three adolescents has an anxiety disorder.
Anxiety has both cognitive and physiological components; both components should be
addressed in assessment of a patient.

Mood and Anxiety Disorders

9/4/26, 9:40 AM
AAOS | Sport Psychology
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000044
4/13

The incidence of mood and anxiety disorder diagnoses has been increasing in young
adults in recent years. Research has consistently indicated a combination of treatment
approaches to result in the best treatment outcomes. Numerous medication options are
available for mood and anxiety disorders. Sport psychiatrists recommend considering
how the adverse effects of a medication (eg, cardiac adverse effects) may affect an
athlete’s performance before prescribing any medication6-8
Injury-related surgical management often contributes to impaired mood. Empirically
validated mood assessments are available for monitoring patients for mood disorders
preoperatively and postoperatively.
Sleep Disorders
Sleep disorders are a major concern in college students and student-athletes.
Sleep disorders are common in the general population and may be a result of the competing
demands in society.
A disruption in routine may result in sleep problems.
Sleep studies and/or consultation with a sleep specialist may aid in the detection and
management of sleep disorders.
Short sleep negatively affects physical and mental health, as well as aerobic, anaerobic, sport-
specific, and cognitive domains of performance.
Sleep disorders are increasing and may lead to impaired mood and performance detriments6,9
(Resource 5).
Concussive Disorders
No preferred standard tests are available for the diagnosis of concussion. Concussion is a
clinical diagnosis; however, early recognition and management is key to improving outcomes.
Concussions may cause mood impairment, worsen an existing mental health condition, or
both.

Concussive Disorders

Concussion management is best provided by a multidisciplinary team of healthcare
professionals. The mental healthcare practitioner is an important part of this team and
may aid in assessing and monitoring mood, providing return to learn recommendations,
and helping the athlete with coping skills (especially for normalizing the stigma
occasionally associated with sport-related concussion)..6
Substance Use/Abuse
Substance abuse is commonly associated with impaired mental health.
Substance use disorders may begin early, can be genetically influenced, and may present
during adolescence.
For some individuals, as few as 7 days of being treated with prescription opiates or
benzodiazipines may result in addiction.
Postinjury, chemical (eg, drug) and process (eg, exercise, gambling) addictive behaviors should
be assessed.

Substance Use/Abuse
Personality traits of high performers may make them more susceptible to substance
abuse. Many factors (biologic, psychologic, social, and spiritual) may increase a person’s
risk of a substance use disorder. Referral to a sport psychology professional is a good
method to track potential changes in mood and substance use in a patient
postoperatively. Preoperative information on substance use and abuse should be
collected to ensure proper medication selection and dosing postoperatively. In addition,
prescribers should be aware of any sport governing body rules related to banned
substances6,10 (Resource 6).
Disordered Eating and Eating Disorders
Diagnosed eating disorders and subclinical disordered eating concerns should be identified,
managed, and monitored.

Disordered eating is one aspect of the female athlete triad (in addition to menstrual
dysfunction and impaired bone health).
Lack of exercise after an injury may affect a patient’s eating patterns and body image.
Emphasis on the thin ideal and the revealing nature of sports’ uniforms may contribute to
disordered eating and eating disorders.

Disordered Eating and Eating Disorders
The term disordered eating indicates subclinical concerns regarding an individual’s
eating behaviors. Disordered eating as a concept is seen in research and literature on
low-energy availability, relative energy deficiency, and the female athlete triad.
Presurgical information on a patient’s nutrition and diet and any indicated body image
concerns should be noted. A change in activity level may lead to changes in body image,
self-perception, and eating habits. In addition, perceived societal pressures may unveil
unhealthy eating habits or disordered eating patterns.6,10
Mental Skills Training
Mental Skills
Goal setting
Visualization/imagery
Relaxation
Mindfulness
Self-talk
Emotional management/regulation

Mental Skills
Mental skills techniques have long been used to optimize sport performance. They can
be used to improve performance in almost any arena. Goal setting is effective in
rehabilitation adherence. Visualization/imagery and relaxation may be helpfulSEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:40 AM
AAOS | Sport Psychology
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000044
7/13

preoperatively to prepare for the demands of surgery and rehabilitation. Mindfulness
has recently gained popularity as a technique a patient can use to focus on the present
and control their emotional space. All mental skills can be trained and improved with
practice.11,12
Mental Skills Training for Injury Rehabilitation
Cognitive appraisal model (Lazarus)
Biopsychosocial approach
Self-determination theory–based intervention
Adherence to rehabilitation
Psychologic readiness to return

Mental Skills Training for Injury Rehabilitation
Multiple frameworks can be used to conceptualize how patients approach injury
rehabilitation. An individual’s perception of how an injury will affect their current
situation or future success may affect their adherence to rehabilitation. Self-
determination theory describes a systemic intervention in which 10 skills are addressed
with patients to increase rehabilitation adherence. A patient’s psychologic state
regarding the injury and desire to return to activity also should be addressed. A patient
may be cleared for but hesitate to return to activity based on psychologic concerns that
they may not be aware of or be ready to discuss11-13 (Resource 7).
Influences on Recovery
Remarkable Recovery
Positive factors
Psychologic growth
Seeing opportunity in challenge


Remarkable Recovery
Remarkable recovery is considered a recovery from an injury and a return to a level of
performance higher than that preinjury or a recovery from an injury thought to be
unrecoverable. Four factors drive remarkable recovery: heightened body awareness,
enhanced pain management, emotional momentum, and a new perspective on sport.
These factors incorporate an element of psychologic growth and an opportunity for a
patient to embrace the opportunity or challenge in their injury situation.11
Stress Response and Pain
Biopsychosocial approach to pain
Allostatic load
Negative effect related to pain tolerance
Fear of pain (and reinjury)
Increased stress response related to injury risk
Cognitive behavioral therapy common treatment strategy

Stress Response and Pain
Surgeons must consider the biologic, psychologic, and social factors that may affect a
patient’s approach to pain. Educating a patient on pain and the importance of a healthy
stress response can facilitate an easier recovery process14
Mental Skills Training for Healthcare Providers
Focused attention
High stress and pressure
Learning and retention of procedures
Routines
Energy management


Mental Skills Training for Healthcare Providers
Mental skills can be useful in numerous settings, including surgery. Similarities exist
among high-performance settings that lead to positive use of mental skills. The high
pressure to perform, need for focused attention and management of energy reserves,
and learned routines are some of those commonalities. Goal setting, imagery, relaxation,
and mindfulness may be beneficial to performance15
